hints: Look at the clear zone around the antibiotic disc. A big zone means bacteria are killed, a shrinking zone means resistant bacteria are growing closer to the disc over the 5 days.
Use the rule given: any diameter less than $13.0\text{ mm}$ means resistance is present. Check each bacteria type, day 1 to day 5, against $13.0\text{ mm}$.
walkthrough:
**Understand what the zone means**

Think of the clear zone as a no-grow area. The antibiotic diffuses out from the disc and stops bacteria growing.

If the diameter stays large, the antibiotic is still working. If it gets smaller, resistant bacteria are surviving and colonising closer to the disc.

**Apply the 13.0 mm resistance rule**

The question tells us: diameter $< 13.0\text{ mm}$ = resistant bacteria present.

Now scan the table:
Type 1: 14.3 to 24.1, all $> 13.0\text{ mm}$, never resistant.
Type 2: falls to 12.2, 9.0, 2.0, so resistant from day 3.
Type 3: falls to 12.8, 12.4, 11.1, 10.9, so resistant from day 2.
Type 4: falls to 8.1, 2.0, so resistant from day 4.
Type 5: stays around 20.4 to 22.0, all $> 13.0\text{ mm}$, never resistant.

**Pick the statement the data supports**

Only types 2, 3 and 4 ever drop below $13.0\text{ mm}$ in these 5 days.

So we can support that only types 2, 3 and 4 show resistance, which is option B.

options.A: Not true. Types 1 and 5 stay above 13.0 mm on all 5 days (14.3 mm and 20.4 mm on day 5), so they show no resistance in this experiment.
options.B: Correct. Types 2, 3 and 4 are the only ones that fall below 13.0 mm, while types 1 and 5 stay well above it for all 5 days.
options.C: Not supported. Type 3 becomes resistant (12.8 mm on day 2), while types 2, 4 and 5 are also still sensitive at the start, so limiting treatment to 1 and 3 is wrong.
options.D: Too strong a claim. The data only shows no resistance in 5 days for type 5, it cannot prove it can never become resistant in the future.
